sn47.42:1.1: This discourse, while doctrinally important, is textually corrupt. It appears to be a fragmentary stub of a text that is more satisfactorily preserved in the Chinese translation at SA 609. The four _satipaṭṭhānas_ are here treated as the objective foundations of meditation, a usage unique in the early texts. The analysis closely parallels that of the five aggregates, as I note below. Nonetheless, the details are carefully distinguished; for example, the singular “feeling” in the aggregates becomes the plural “feelings” here.
sn47.42:1.3: This question appears rather oddly here. SA 609, rather, asks “What is the origination and cessation of the four kinds of mindfulness meditation”, then explains them, then rounds off by saying it has answered the question.
sn47.42:1.4: The same statement is said of “form” (_rūpa_) at [sn22.56:3.4]() and [sn22.57:2.4]().
sn47.42:1.5: While the specified origin and ending are the same, the Chinese text fills out each section by saying that one who meditates observing origin and ending will be independent and not grasp anything in the world. This passage is similar to one found in the Satipaṭṭhānasutta, but not elsewhere in the Pali ([mn10:5.3]()).
sn47.42:1.6: Also at [sn22.56:6.5]() and [sn22.57:6.6](). Here the plural form is specified.
sn47.42:1.8: Said of “consciousness” at [sn22.56:13.5]() and [sn22.57:14.5](). While “mind” (_citta_) and “consciousness” (_viññāṇa_) are synonyms, _citta_ is typically used in the context of practice, while _viññāṇa_ is used in the context of understanding.
